activities.anchor: Why does salt spilled on a lawn kill the grass
activities.caption: bet on the tree's secret before you read on
activities.name: pcvSaltPredict

config.q: A tree holds a crown of leaves two hundred feet up — with no bones and no steel. What is doing the structural work?
choices: Mineral deposits, like a shell, laid down inside every trunk
Water pressure inside cells pushing outward against stiff cellulose walls
Suction from the roots pulling the crown down tight
config.why: The plant skeleton is hydraulic: walls inflated by water — the same pressurised box that keeps lettuce crisp and explains the salt on the lawn.

activities.anchor: tiny solar panels that capture sunlight
activities.caption: pair each invention with the job it does
activities.name: pcvInventionMatch

config.prompt: Pair each plant-only invention with its job:

pairs.right: the standing skeleton — strong fibres in a soft matrix
manufacture sugar from light, air and water
storage, waste and water pressure in one sac

config.why: Animals buy the same jobs with organs — skeleton, gut, liver, kidneys — while the plant cell does all three inside the one box.

activities.caption: drag the divider — same problems, two solutions
activities.name: pcvAnimalPlantCompare

config.prompt: Animal way vs plant way — drag the divider across the card:

before.label: animals
before.text: Skeletons of mineral and protein inside the body; eat by moving and digest inside a gut; keep storage and waste in dedicated organs — liver, kidneys, fat.

after.label: plants
after.text: Walls inflated by water — a water skeleton, like a garden hose that stiffens when full; stay put and manufacture sugar from light, air and water; one sac does warehouse, recycling and poison locker at once.

config.why: Each invention answers a problem animals solve differently — and the rest of the toolkit, nucleus to mitochondria, is the same kit your cells carry.

activities.caption: build the primary wall from the sugar up
activities.name: pcvWallOrder

config.prompt: Build a primary wall, from sugar upward:
items: Chains bond side by side into crystalline cables — microfibrils
Cables woven through a wet matrix of hemicelluloses and pectins
The laminate is secreted as the primary wall of a young cell
config.why: Weight for weight the cellulose cables have tensile strength comparable to steel — strong fibres in a soft matrix, like fibreglass.

activities.caption: file the plastid family by costume
activities.name: pcvPlastidBuckets

config.prompt: One genome, three costumes. File each plastid job:

items.label: carotenoids unveiled as chlorophyll is dismantled
starch grains stockpiled in a potato

config.why: All descended from the same swallowed bacterium and interconvertible from proplastids — plant 'green' is a state, not an identity: every plastid-bearing cell can change costume.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — where a tree's mass comes from
activities.name: pcvAirCloze

config.text: Soil supplies %%0%% and a handful of minerals; the bulk of a plant's dry weight is %%1%% pulled from the air as %%2%% and built into sugar by chloroplasts. Weigh a tree against the pot of soil it stands in, and the soil barely changes.
config.hint: Look up, not down, for where the mass came from.

activities.anchor: crunchy celery, crisp lettuce and upright annuals
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the internal skeleton
activities.name: pcvTurgorEstimate

config.prompt: A living leaf cell holds a turgor pressure of roughly how many atmospheres (a car tyre runs at 2–3)?
config.why: Routinely 5–10 atmospheres — two to four car tyres' worth of internal skeleton, all of it the wall pushing back.
config.context: That reciprocal push is what inflates a leaf like a football — and what falls when it wilts.

activities.caption: one line of the plasmolysis walkthrough is wrong
activities.name: pcvPlasmolysisSpot

config.prompt: One line of this water-potential walkthrough is wrong. Find it.
lines: A cell with concentrated vacuole sap has low water potential, so water enters until pressure raises its potential to match the surroundings
The surroundings are made saltier — sea water, fertiliser overdose, salad dressing
Dissolved solutes lower the outside water potential
The outside potential now sits above the cell's, so water flows into the cell
The membrane pulls away from the wall — plasmolysis — and the tissue wilts
config.correction: The outside potential now sits below the cell's, so water flows out of the cell.
config.why: Solutes lower potential: saltier outside means water leaves, not enters — the same physics reversed opens stomata each morning.
